questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The location was crucial - I wanted to go to to a place in East Asia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a little difficult to find information online and in English. The counsellor also did not reply to my emails that I sent which made it difficult to ask for help because she was the only contact we had.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an orientation and tour.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were single rooms that were around 8 mins from the entrance of campus and a four person "on-campus" accommodation that was actually 45 mins away. For single rooms, there were suite options that were slightly more expensive but had a shared common room and kitchen between 5 people.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were very few dorms that had access to a shared kitchen. Otherwise there were no cooking facilities in the rooms. There was a microwave and small oven in the lobby otherwise.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The communication may not be very clear and the lobby attendants are very stressed during move in dates so they may not be so patient. Some of them do not speak English too - but there is always someone in the lobby.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There were several rounds of applying for courses over a span of a few weeks so there was a possibility of trying out a class before dropping it or applying for it. If you couldn't get into a class you wanted, you had to find out where the class was held and attend the lecture to ask the teacher if you could join the class, otherwise find an email.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There weren't many resources or guides - it was mostly other students that knew the system more and we talked about it amongst ourselves.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in arranging for the classes I wanted that fit my schedule.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you hang on to credits just in case you don't get into the class you want, the system will not prioritise you for the next rounds if you want to change class.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses are quite rigorous, especially if it is math involved. Otherwise there is usually a lot of reading for social sciences and the teachers expect you to participate or do assignments to show that you have done the reading and this counts as part of the grade.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teachers had a lot of power to change the course - there were several instances of the teacher just changing the syllabus or grading system during the course. They also take attendance and participation as part of the grade. It is wholly up to the teacher to set the rubrics and your grade as they want and it was difficult at times to know exactly what they are looking for as some teachers are quite strict in class but lenient with the grading.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:

Mini-course: European Union and State Transformation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Political Communication in the Internet Age

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: A lot of things for the dorm.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: With the food prices being relatively low, drinks at a cafe can get pricey.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were many many options - such as volleyball, golf, archery, martial arts, art, calligraphy, hiking, etc., but it could be hard to be part of the club community if you didn't speak Mandarin and most things are conducted in Chinese.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking could be a good one for exploration.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: It is quite easy to travel along the places on the high speed rail so that's very doable for the weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was not so difficult because I also come from an Asian culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: A lot of students are quite shy so you would probably have to take initiative and approach them to make plans first. Otherwise, everyone is quite friendly. There could be a language barrier though because some people are not comfortable with speaking English all the time.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It can be difficult with the assumptions people make based on the way you dress or look. Also, no food or drink on the metro.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciate how friendly people were and are willing to help.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't worry too much about grades, the teachers may seem strict with the grading in class but most are understanding and don't grade you harshly.
2. Try different foods, Taiwan has a lot to offer and lots of street food as well. 
3. You will mostly be in classes with other internationals - so if you want more of the local experience you have to work harder for it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I wanted a multiple entry visa and paid 660 to get it and only ended up with 90 days. Some others got 90 day single entry or 180. It really depends on the person giving it to you. A 90 visa is fine, you can extend it there and it won't affect your entry in the country - I always explained that I will extend and ended up travelling multiple times out of the country anyway, which extended it because I got 90 days visa exempt (but you have to tell the stamp person that you want visa exempt and not part of multiple entry to get the 90 days extended).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was rewarding to experience living and studying in another country - making friends there was also a great experience. I took a violin class and ended up getting the chance to do a short performance as well. I would say take the chances that come to you with doing what you like.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was challenging finding information about all the processes and the documents and information also came quite late to do the applications. Also, you only knew if you were getting a dorm in July if you applied for it so I was also looking for housing just in case I couldn't get a dorm - a lot of extra work if you did end up getting a dorm.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
